title: Design a URL Shortener
summary: Blank canvas. 12,000 requests per second, 95% of them redirects. Build it fast, reliable and affordable.
scenario: You're building a link shortener. Users create short links (writes) and millions of people click them (reads that redirect to the long URL).
Peak traffic is 12,000 requests per second. Reads outnumber writes 19 to 1, and popular links get clicked far more than the rest: 80% of redirects hit a small set of hot links.
Start from an empty canvas. A redirect should feel instant, the service must survive any single failure, and finance wants the bill under $2,000 a month.

functional: Create a short link for a long URL
Redirect a short link to its long URL
nonFunctional: Handle 12,000 requests/s at peak, 19 reads per write
80% of redirects hit a small set of hot links
Redirects feel instant: average latency at or below 60 ms
Database load at or below 4,000 rps

objectives.label: Average latency at or below 60 ms
Database load at or below 4,000 rps

hints: Start with the request path: Client, then Load Balancer, then App Servers, then a datastore. Run it and let the bottlenecks tell you what to scale.
A short code maps to one long URL: a pure key-value lookup with no joins. A NoSQL store scales reads and writes with shards. Redirects of hot links should be answered by a cache before reaching it.

One app server handles 1,500 rps, so 12,000 rps needs at least 8, and around 12 for headroom. Give the load balancer, cache and database 2 replicas each to remove single points of failure, and add Monitoring.
explanation: A strong baseline: Client → Load Balancer (×2) → stateless App Servers (×12) → Redis Cache (×2, ~32 GB) in front of a sharded NoSQL store (×2), plus Monitoring.
Why NoSQL: the access pattern is get(shortCode) and put(shortCode, longUrl). No joins and no multi-row transactions, and both reads and writes need to scale horizontally. Partition by short code.
Why the cache: with 80% of clicks on hot links, a large cache absorbs roughly 80% of redirect reads, cutting database load from ~11,400 to ~2,100 rps and lowering latency.

Things the simulator doesn't model but an interviewer will ask about: generating unique short codes (counter with base62, or pre-allocated ranges), custom aliases, link expiry, abuse and rate limiting, and analytics. Click counts belong on an async queue so they never slow down the redirect.
